column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
A parent passes something to its child and the child adds something of its own. What does each generation contribute to the differences seen in the next?
Why would a field of sugarcane plants look much more uniform than a crowd of people?
A heat wave hits two groups of bacteria, one with heat tolerance and one without. What difference would you expect afterwards?
What role does the surroundings play in deciding which variants become more common over time?
A child resembles both parents in some ways and neither exactly. What general principles explain how traits are passed on?
How many copies of the instructions for a single trait does a child hold, and where did each come from?
What kind of plants did Mendel get when he crossed a tall pea plant with a short one, and what did this rule out?
If all first-generation plants look tall, where does a dwarf plant in the next generation come from?
In a plant carrying two different versions of a gene for height, which version shows up and what do we call each version?
After crossing a tall round-seeded plant with a short wrinkled-seeded one, what do all the first-generation plants look like?
What do the tall-wrinkled and short-round plants in the second generation tell us about whether the two traits travel together?
What exactly does a stretch of the cell's genetic material hold information for, and what do we call such a stretch?
Two pea plants differ in height only because of a small change in one gene. Explain step by step how that change ends up affecting height.
If a body cell holds two sets of genes, how many sets must each egg or sperm hold, and why?
Why does it matter that the genetic material is in separate pieces rather than one long strand, when we think about traits being passed on independently?
What stops the number of chromosomes from doubling or halving over the generations?
Name an animal whose sex depends on how warm its eggs are kept and another that can change its sex during its life.
Is a human baby's sex decided by the temperature of its surroundings, or by something else, and what is that something?
How many chromosome pairs are alike in everyone, and how does the last pair differ between a woman and a man?
A couple has a baby. What does the mother always pass on, and which parent's contribution decides the baby's sex?
